Gina / team — attaching a conservative sizing write-up and the workbook Marissa referenced. Key assumptions up front:

Assumptions (pilot -> prod):
- Pilot: 10 qps peak, 8 concurrent active users (chat-style interactive sessions), avg sequence length 350 tokens, tail to 1k tokens for some long cases.
- Year-1 Prod (single US region): 120 qps peak, 60 concurrent sessions, average sequence length 300 tokens.
- Model family: customer prefers a 33B-70B family for quality; we size for 70B-class model (quantized to 4-bit / q4) for headroom. If they accept 33B quantized, footprint drops ~45%.
- Target latency SLO: p95 <= 220ms for streaming responses; some ops allowed for p95 up to 400ms for long context requests.
- KV/prefix cache hit assumed at 25% for interactive workflows, can be higher with prompt engineering.

Sizing summary (order of magnitude):
- Dedicated (Redwood-managed isolated pool):
  - Pilot: 2 nodes of H100-equivalent (each node = 8x80GB-equivalent GPU with NVLink), allowing batching and some burst capacity. Handles 10 qps with comfortable headroom.
  - Year-1 Prod: 8–10 nodes of H100-equivalent (estimate ~64–80 GPUs total depending on model & batching). Enables autoscaling policy with reserved baseline (6 nodes) and burst lanes.
  - Advantages: faster onboarding (2–4 weeks), lower engineering lift, predictable per-token economics once commit signed.

- Private (Customer VPC or on-prem air-gap):
  - Pilot: 2x 80GB A100 or 4x 40GB GPUs (depending on customer procurement). Network & storage validated by customer; Redwood provides control-plane connectors.
  - Year-1 Prod: equivalent of 10–12 x 80GB-class GPUs (on-prem) OR a dedicated VPC reserved pool of similar size. Need to account for redundancy (N+1), maintenance windows, and cross-site failover for DR.
  - Advantages: Customer data never leaves their network if air-gapped; full KMS/HSM control; preferred for certain contracts requiring customer-managed keys.

Operational notes that affect sizing/cost:
- Quantization: moving to q4 reduces memory and GPU count materially; q8/int8 savings are less pronounced for latency SLOs.
- Batching windows: Dedicated can use continuous batching and request-shaping at the infra layer; Private may need tighter SLAs on batch latency based on customer networking.
- Caching: Effective prefix/KV caching can reduce steady-state GPU needs by 15–30% on query-heavy workflows.

Security/compliance differences:
- Audit logs: Both options provide equivalent audit-grade logs; Private option can stream logs into customer SIEM behind their network boundary.
- KMS/HSM: Dedicated supports customer-managed keys via cloud KMS integrations; Private supports on-prem HSM and firewall rules.
- Patching & maintenance: Dedicated follows Redwood-managed patch schedule (monthly security releases + emergency patches). Private can opt into Redwood-managed patch orchestration or run at customer cadence (longer lead time).

Cost bands (very high level monthly committed):
- Dedicated: Pilot ~$35k–$60k/month; Year-1 committed band ~$250k–$420k/month (depends on GPU mix, retention, and support tier).
- Private: Pilot (capex) depends on hardware procurement; operational equivalent monthly run-rate (managed turnkey) ~$320k–$500k/month plus one-time integration/installation (~$60k–$180k depending on on-prem complexity).

I'll attach the workbook with node-level assumptions and a per-GPU token cost row. We should confirm model acceptance (33B vs 70B) with Gina — that changes counts a lot.
